USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Keep the existing Section 301 tariff stack in place and press the April text work to a written, enforceable deal—especially IP, forced tech transfer, and a snap-back enforcement mechanism—without raising List 3 to 25% and without rolling tariffs back first. Use the next few weeks of video and principal-level talks to lock structural language before any Xi summit is scheduled. Do not trade Meng/Huawei for purchase pledges, and do not accept a purchases-only settlement.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The dispute is not an existential threat to U.S. interests as of 24 April 2019; it is a leverage window with a contained but real domestic cost. After the 2018 tariff cascade (Lists 1–3 covering ~$250B at 10–25%) and matching Chinese retaliation, the G20 90-day pause and the 24 February delay of the List 3 hike shifted the contest from escalation into bargaining (timeline 2018-12-01, 2019-02-24, 2019-04-03). April Washington talks produced draft text on IP, tech transfer, agriculture, services, purchases and enforcement, but Lighthizer still flagged “major, major issues” and USTR said “significant work remains”—so the opportunity is to extract structural concessions, not to declare victory (VOA 4 Apr; Guardian/USTR 7 Apr). Macro data back a mild-opportunity reading rather than high threat: VIX ~13, Michigan sentiment back near 97, CNY firmer at ~6.72, and China still growing industrial output ~5.4% YoY with stable reserves—i.e., Beijing is not collapsing, but neither is the U.S. in a tariff-driven recession (country_health). The offsetting harm is concentrated: U.S. goods exports to China are down, IMPCH is ~26% lower, 2018 ag exports to China were less than half prior years, and USDA estimated large unsold soybean stocks and a ~$1.9B farm-export hit (farmdoc 12 Apr; USDA/Hill Feb). Advisers already blocked a premature summit announcement because it would weaken leverage (NYT via Farm Policy News). Escalating tariffs now would likely break the most constructive negotiating stretch of the year and deepen farm/manufacturing pain; conceding purchases or a partial rollback before enforcement is written would give away the remaining U.S. bargaining chip. Negotiate—hold the tariffs, finish the text.
key_factors: April 2019 talks have draft text but no signed deal; enforcement and remaining tariffs are the end-game
List 3 hike to 25% remains suspended; existing ~$250B Section 301 coverage is the main U.S. lever
U.S. macro is stable (low VIX, recovered sentiment); China is not in acute distress
Farm-belt retaliation is the clearest U.S. cost (soybeans, ag export collapse to China)
Huawei/Meng track is live but should stay legally separate from a commercial settlement
Premature summit or unilateral rollback would weaken leverage before structural commitments are locked

sources_cited.excerpt: List 3 takes effect at 10%. China imposes retaliatory tariffs (5–10%) on ~$60B of US goods. Combined US Section 301 coverage now ~$250B of Chinese imports.
G20 Buenos Aires dinner: Trump and Xi agree to a 90-day negotiation window. Planned Jan 1, 2019 hike of List 3 from 10% to 25% is suspended.
Trump tweets that talks have made substantial progress and further delays the scheduled List 3 hike from 10% to 25%.
Intensive Washington talks between US and Chinese negotiators; both sides report progress on text, including enforcement language. No final deal signed.
VIX latest 13.14 on 2019-04-24, down ~47% over the window — markets are pricing low stress, not a crisis.
Michigan consumer sentiment 97.2 in April 2019 after a January dip to 91.2 — household confidence has recovered.
U.S. goods imports from China down to $34.5B in April 2019 from $46.3B in November 2018 (−26%).
U.S. goods exports to China $7.9B in April 2019, still below late-2018 levels and well below pre-war run-rates.
Trump (4 Apr 2019): getting closer, possible announcement in ~four weeks; Lighthizer: still some major, major issues left. No deal signed.
USTR: significant work remains on IP, forced tech transfer, NTBs, agriculture, services, purchases and enforcement; talks continue by video.
2018 U.S. agricultural exports to China were less than half the prior three years; China 25% soybean tariff hit the dominant U.S. farm customer.
Trade advisers blocked a pre-deal summit announcement as weakening U.S. leverage; farm/manufacturing pressure to resolve is rising.
